importance_evaluation.scientific_significance: Formulated the fundamental laws of classical mechanics, universal gravitation, optics, and independently developed infinitesimal calculus, laying the theoretical foundation of modern classical physics.
importance_evaluation.historical_significance: Key central figure of the 17th-century Scientific Revolution whose 1687 publication Principia Mathematica unified celestial and terrestrial mechanics under a single mathematical paradigm.

timeline_a_biological.event: Born at Woolsthorpe Manor, Lincolnshire (January 4, 1643 New Style / December 25, 1642 Old Style).
timeline_a_biological.evidence_note: Recorded in local parish registers; date variations stem from Julian vs. Gregorian calendars.

timeline_a_biological.event: Entered Trinity College, Cambridge as a sizar.
Graduated B.A.; returned to Woolsthorpe due to the Great Plague outbreak at Cambridge.
timeline_a_biological.evidence_note: Cambridge University records and Newton's personal notebooks.

timeline_a_biological.event: Appointed Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge succeeding Isaac Barrow.
timeline_a_biological.evidence_note: Official appointment records at Trinity College.

timeline_a_biological.event: Moved to London to become Warden of the Royal Mint; later promoted to Master of the Mint in 1699.
timeline_a_biological.evidence_note: Royal Mint historical records and official correspondence.

timeline_a_biological.event: Elected President of the Royal Society, holding the post until his death.
Knighted by Queen Anne at Trinity College, Cambridge.
Died in London on March 31, 1727 (NS) / March 20, 1726/27 (OS) and buried in Westminster Abbey.
timeline_a_biological.evidence_note: Westminster Abbey burial records and contemporary obituaries.

timeline_b_scientific.description: Annus Mirabilis: Developed early concepts of calculus (fluxions), optical experiments with prisms, and initial ideas on gravity.
timeline_b_scientific.evidence_note: Newton's 'Waste Book' and private manuscripts dated 1665-1666.

timeline_b_scientific.description: Constructed the first practical reflecting telescope (Newtonian reflector).
timeline_b_scientific.evidence_note: Presented to the Royal Society in late 1671.

timeline_b_scientific.description: Published 'New Theory about Light and Colors' in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society.
Published 'Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica' setting forth three laws of motion and universal gravitation.
timeline_b_scientific.evidence_note: First edition published by the Royal Society under Edmond Halley's supervision.

timeline_b_scientific.description: Published 'Opticks: or, a Treatise of the Reflexions, Refractions, Inflexions and Colours of Light'.
timeline_b_scientific.evidence_note: First English edition published in London.

physics_analysis.historical_claim: Every point mass attracts every other point mass in the universe by a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
physics_analysis.scientific_problem: Explaining both planetary motion (Kepler's laws) and terrestrial free-fall under a single unified mathematical force law.
physics_analysis.historical_hypothesis: Gravitational attraction extends indefinitely from Earth to the Moon and planets, decreasing with the inverse square of distance.
physics_analysis.historical_model_or_framework: Geometrical dynamic model utilizing limits, geometric proportions, and inverse-square attraction acting central to masses.
physics_analysis.modern_interpretation: A classical non-relativistic force law accurate for weak gravitational fields and speeds much lower than the speed of light; understood as a weak-field limit of General Relativity.
physics_analysis.experiment_details: Mathematical deduction combining lunar orbit data, Kepler's third law, and terrestrial pendulum experiments; later experimentally confirmed directly by Cavendish (1798).

variables_definition.G: Gravitational constant (introduced explicitly in modern formulation)

equations.validity_domain: Classical non-relativistic mechanics in weak gravitational fields
equations.assumptions: Spherical bodies with uniform mass distribution act as point masses; non-relativistic speeds; Euclidean space

physics_analysis.result_and_impact: Successfully derived Kepler's three laws of planetary motion, explained oceanic tides, and unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics.
physics_analysis.limitations_and_boundary_conditions: Fails in strong gravitational fields, high speeds approaching light, or precise anomalies such as Mercury's perihelion precession.
physics_analysis.verification_note: Newton expressed relationships via geometric proportions rather than modern algebraic notation with an explicit gravitational constant G.

physics_analysis.historical_claim: Formulated the foundational laws governing body inertia, force acceleration relation, and action-reaction pairs.
physics_analysis.scientific_problem: Lack of a rigorous mechanical foundation to describe inertia, force, and dynamic interactions of physical bodies.
physics_analysis.historical_hypothesis: Motion changes only when acted upon by net external forces, and force is proportional to the rate of change of motion (momentum).
physics_analysis.historical_model_or_framework: Axiomatic classical mechanics framework presented in the Principia Mathematica.
physics_analysis.modern_interpretation: The foundational dynamic laws of Newtonian mechanics, valid in inertial frames for macroscopic objects moving at non-relativistic speeds.
physics_analysis.experiment_details: Synthesized observational data on pendulums, collisions, falling bodies, and astronomical orbits.

equations.validity_domain: Inertial reference frames at non-relativistic speeds
equations.assumptions: Constant mass system, classical space and time metrics

physics_analysis.result_and_impact: Established classical mechanics as an exact mathematical science, defining concepts of force, mass, and momentum.
physics_analysis.limitations_and_boundary_conditions: Inapplicable at quantum scales or near light speed; requires modification in non-inertial frames via fictitious forces.
physics_analysis.verification_note: Newton defined 'quantity of motion' as momentum (mass times velocity); F = ma is Euler's later algebraic formulation.

physics_analysis.contribution_name: Decomposition of White Light and Spectrum Theory
physics_analysis.historical_claim: White light is not simple and homogeneous, but a heterogeneous mixture of refrangible rays corresponding to distinct colors.
physics_analysis.scientific_problem: Prevailing Aristotelian view held that color was a modification of pure white light caused by glass or medium.
physics_analysis.historical_hypothesis: Prisms separate light into constituent spectral colors based on their varying differential refrangibility.
physics_analysis.historical_model_or_framework: Corpuscular / particle theory of light combined with optical refraction analysis.
physics_analysis.modern_interpretation: White light consists of a continuous spectrum of electromagnetic wavelengths, each bending differently in dispersive media according to its refractive index.
physics_analysis.experiment_details: Experimentum Crucis: Isolated a single colored ray passing through a first prism and directed it through a second prism; the color did not change further, proving refrangibility was an intrinsic property of the light ray.
physics_analysis.result_and_impact: Revolutionized optical science, led to the design of reflecting telescopes free from chromatic aberration, and established modern optics.
physics_analysis.limitations_and_boundary_conditions: Newton's corpuscular light hypothesis failed to explain wave phenomena like diffraction and interference without complex secondary assumptions.
physics_analysis.verification_note: Well documented in his 1672 Royal Society paper and detailed in 'Opticks' (1704).

major_claims_audit.recommended_wording: Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz independently developed calculus, Newton focusing on fluxions and Leibniz developing the modern differential/integral notation.

major_claims_audit.claim: An apple fell on Newton's head, causing him to instantly discover universal gravity.
major_claims_audit.recommended_wording: Newton recalled being inspired to think about gravity while observing an apple fall from a tree, but universal gravitation was developed through years of rigorous mathematical analysis.

major_claims_audit.claim: Newton formulated F = ma explicitly in his Principia.
major_claims_audit.recommended_wording: Newton stated the second law in words as proportional change in momentum; the modern equation F = ma was later explicitly written by Leonhard Euler.

verified_sources.title: Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica
verified_sources.supported_claim: Formulation of the three laws of motion and universal gravitation.

verified_sources.title: Opticks: or, a Treatise of the Reflexions, Refractions, Inflexions and Colours of Light
verified_sources.supported_claim: Prism experiments, spectrum decomposition, and corpuscular optical theory.

verified_sources.title: Never at Rest: A Biography of Isaac Newton
verified_sources.supported_claim: Comprehensive biographical dates, priority priority disputes, and academic chronology.

major_uncertainties: Exact timeline of private early fluxion notes during 1665-1666 plague years relative to Leibniz's independent discoveries.
high_risk_claims: Attributing the modern equation F=ma directly to Newton without clarifying his original momentum formulation.
Over-simplifying the priority dispute over calculus between Newton and Leibniz.
